name: Carlos Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm based at the Plainsview depot, on the flat farmland east of the city, and my speciality is storm restoration. When a big storm flattens lines anywhere in our area, or in the next region over, I'm on the first crew sent to rebuild. In between storms it's ordinary work, replacing poles and rebuilding old lines. But the storms are what I'm known for. I've rebuilt forty kilometres of line in a week after a tornado.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving a mess. You arrive, it's all poles snapped like matchsticks, and you work out the order to put it back. I use AI every day, for weather maps, for planning which section to rebuild first, even for checking my rental properties' accounts. What wears me out is the sleeping in motels for two weeks at a time. I'm fifty-eight, my back likes my own bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, and anyone who isn't using it is leaving time on the table. At work I'd keep showing the younger guys how I plan a rebuild with it. Online I'd say, well, the hype was too big, but the tool is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. I've got two rental houses, savings, a pension coming, and I'd planned to finish at sixty-two. If the world stays the same, my plan stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the job and the AI tools I already use. I'd keep looking for small ways it saves time on storm planning and suggest them to the depot manager. I'd keep the rentals ticking over and put spare money into shares like I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I like new things. I thought I'd see something amazing before I retired. But my wife Amira would be pleased, she thinks I spend too much time on my phone already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the rental houses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Tenants pay, I fix the boiler when it breaks, the mortgage on the second one is nearly done. AI helps me with the paperwork. Nothing changes there.

S0.say: It's still a good tool, and anyone not using it is leaving time on the table. The hype was too big, but the tool is real.
S0.think: For me nothing much changes, with two rental houses, savings and a pension coming. If the world stays the same, my plan to finish at sixty-two stays the same.
S0.do: Carries on with the job and the AI tools he already uses, suggesting small time savings in storm planning to his manager. Keeps the rental houses running and puts spare money into shares as usual.
S0.quote: I thought I'd see something amazing before I retired. But my wife Amira would be pleased, she thinks I spend too much time on my phone already.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is a practical problem-solver who enjoys technology and has built up property and savings. Nothing in this scenario threatens him. If anything he'd miss the excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. At work I'd tell the young ones to get good with drones and the planning software, because that's where the work goes. I'm not one to complain about change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's an opportunity. My son-in-law Sami is an electrician, my son Yusuf's an engineer. If inspection and planning go to drones and software, there's money in running that for smaller power companies who can't do it themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my commercial drone licence and help Sami get his too. I'd put maybe a fifth of our savings into a small drone inspection business with him, doing contract work for co-ops and solar farms. I'd keep my day job and work on the business at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually excited. It's the kind of change a man can make something of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about this business idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small power companies and solar farms need their lines and panels checked every year. They don't want to hire a full crew. We'd fly a drone, let the software spot faults, and send a report. Sami does the electrical side, I know the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't some people say the companies are taking jobs away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will. But nobody owes anybody a job forever. If there's new work, go and get it. That's what my father did when he came here with nothing, and he did all right.

S1.say: This is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. Get good with drones and planning software, because that's where the work goes.
S1.think: I think it's an opportunity. If inspection and planning go to drones and software, there's money in running that for smaller power companies that can't do it themselves.
S1.do: Gets a commercial drone licence in the first year and helps his son-in-law get one too. Puts about a fifth of the family savings into a small drone inspection business with him, run at weekends alongside his day job.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, seeing a chance to build something.
S1.quote: Nobody owes anybody a job forever. If there's new work, go and get it.
S1.fieldNote: He immediately sees a business opportunity and has a family partner ready. His free-market view is shaped by his father's story of starting with nothing. He's comfortable risking part of his savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready fast, and don't wait for anyone to save you. At work I'd tell the crew to learn whatever they can and to save money. I'd say it at the mosque too, to the younger men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'm sixty in 2028, I've got the rentals and savings. But two years means everything I'd planned slowly has to happen now, and in a rush you make mistakes. And I'd worry the business I'd build gets overtaken in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the company early and put my time into the business with Sami straight away. I'd buy the robots or drones myself rather than wait for others, because whoever owns the machines does well. I'd put some savings into the companies making them as well. I'd keep the rentals, because people still need a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's like a storm that moves faster than the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. Does your drone business idea still work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If AI can do the whole job, even the inspection reports, then a small business doesn't have much of an edge. The edge might be owning the machines and the contracts. That's why I'd buy rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young men at the mosque and on the crew who don't have savings. People who did everything right, learned a trade, and now it's gone in two years. I'd want to help them find something, give some of them work if the business does well.

S2.say: Get ready fast and don't wait for anyone to save you. Learn whatever you can and save money.
S2.think: I'd be fine, at sixty in 2028 with the rentals and savings. But everything I'd planned slowly would have to happen in a rush, and in a rush you make mistakes.
S2.do: Leaves the company early to put his time into the business with his son-in-law right away, buying robots or drones himself rather than waiting. Puts some savings into the companies making the machines and keeps the rental houses.
S2.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, like a storm moving faster than forecast.
S2.quote: Whoever owns the machines does well.
S2.fieldNote: He responds to the fastest change by trying to own part of it, which fits his outlook and appetite for risk. His unease is about rushed decisions rather than money. He shows a strong sense of duty to younger men in his community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so get moving. I'd tell the young crew to use the time to learn and to save, and not to expect a handout. A few years is plenty if you start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the one that suits me best. I'm sixty-three by 2031, so I can build the business properly while I still have my job, then hand it over to Sami and Yusuf. It's good timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the drone business with Sami in the first year, at weekends, and grow it slowly. I'd take a course on robot maintenance, because someone will have to keep the machines running. I'd move some savings into shares in the companies making grid robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a fair race, and I like a fair race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it right. Test the business, find the customers, make the mistakes when they're cheap. With two years I'd be gambling. With five I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage your son and son-in-law to go all in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami, yes. Yusuf has a good job in engineering, and he can decide for himself. I'd tell them both: don't put in more than you can lose, but don't sit still.

S3.say: We've been warned, so get moving. A few years is plenty if you start now, and nobody should expect a handout.
S3.think: I think this is the one that suits me best. I'm sixty-three by 2031, so I can build the business properly while I still have my job, then hand it over to Sami and Yusuf.
S3.do: Starts the drone business with his son-in-law at weekends in the first year and grows it slowly. Takes a robot maintenance course and moves some savings into shares in companies making grid robots.
S3.feel: Calm, like it's a fair race.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be gambling. With five I'm building.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up neatly with his retirement and his business plan. He frames the difference in timing as gambling versus building. He'd advise his family to take risks they can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. If you can't get ready in ten years, that's on you. I'd tell young people to learn the machines and to start something of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be retired, maybe still part-owner of the business with Sami. I think this could be good for families who prepare. The ones who don't prepare will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-two as planned. I'd start the business slowly, maybe in a few years, and let Sami run it. I'd keep investing in shares and keep the rentals, and help the kids with whatever they decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, in my own bed every night, which is the dream. Maybe sitting on the business's board, giving advice nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people will waste it. Ten years is long enough to think you have time. It's the same with storms. The forecast says it's coming next week and people still don't buy batteries until the night before.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and if you can't get ready in ten years, that's on you. Learn the machines and start something of your own.
S4.think: I'd be retired by then, maybe still part-owner of the business with Sami. I think this could be good for families who prepare, and the ones who don't will struggle.
S4.do: Keeps working to sixty-two as planned and starts the business slowly, letting his son-in-law run it. Keeps investing in shares and the rental houses, and helps his children with whatever they decide.
S4.quote: The forecast says it's coming next week and people still don't buy batteries until the night before.
S4.fieldNote: He sees the long version as easy for anyone who plans ahead. His storm work shapes how he thinks about warning time. He's comfortable and optimistic, if a bit hard on those who don't prepare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, but not for me. For the young men with no savings and a trade that vanishes overnight. What would help is employers and communities finding them work fast, apprenticeships in the new jobs, not just cheques.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd tell the robot. I'd tell it the order. Every storm rebuild, you do the hospital first, then the water pumps, then the farms with animals. If the machine doesn't know that, it doesn't know the job.

headlineQuote: Every storm rebuild, you do the hospital first, then the water pumps, then the farms with animals.
portrait: Carlos Ibrahim is a 58-year-old storm restoration lineworker from a farmland depot who once rebuilt forty kilometres of line in a week after a tornado. He uses AI every day, owns two rental houses and shares, and sees most change as a chance to build something, in his case a drone inspection business with his electrician son-in-law Sami. He stays calm in every scenario except AGI by 2028, where he is uneasy about rushing his plans and worried for young men without savings. His father's story of arriving with nothing shapes his belief that nobody owes anyone a job forever. He'd rather own the machines than fight them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for himself but for young men with no savings whose trade could vanish almost overnight.
whatWouldHelp: Employers and communities finding those young men work quickly, with apprenticeships in the new jobs rather than just cheques.
